questions.question: On a coordinate grid of the school field, a marker cone sits at P(-4, 3). Mr. Chan slides it 6 units right and 5 units down. What are the coordinates of the image P'?
questions.explain: For a translation, add to x when you move right and subtract from y when you move down: (-4 + 6, 3 - 5) = (2, -2). The usual trap is moving the wrong way — left instead of right, or up instead of down — so say the direction out loud as you change each coordinate.

questions.question: Point A(5, -2) is reflected in the x-axis. What are the coordinates of A'?
questions.explain: A reflection in the x-axis keeps x the same and flips the sign of y: (5, -2) becomes (5, 2). The most common mistake is flipping the x-coordinate instead — that is a reflection in the y-axis, a different mirror line.

questions.question: Which regular polygon can tile a floor all by itself, with no gaps and no overlaps?
questions.explain: A regular shape tessellates only when its angle divides exactly into 360°, and 360° ÷ 120° = 3 hexagons meet at each point. The trap is picking a shape whose angle 'nearly' fits, like the pentagon: 3 × 108° = 324°, which leaves a 36° gap.

questions.question: Aria is designing a spinning logo for her hockey team. On her grid, one corner of the logo is at B(3, 5). She rotates the logo 90° clockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of B'?
questions.explain: For a 90° clockwise turn about the origin, swap the coordinates and then change the sign of the new y: (3, 5) becomes (5, -3). Many students swap the numbers but forget the sign change, or turn counterclockwise by mistake — check that the image really landed in the quadrant you expect.

questions.question: Triangle DEF has vertices D(2, 1), E(5, 1) and F(2, 3). Its image has vertices D'(-2, -1), E'(-5, -1) and F'(-2, -3). Which single transformation was used?
options: A translation of 4 units left and 2 units down
A rotation of 180° about the origin
questions.explain: Both coordinates of every vertex changed sign, which is exactly the rule for a 180° rotation about the origin. The classic trap is testing only D, where a translation of 4 left and 2 down also works — always check every vertex before you decide.

questions.question: Liam is making a mosaic border for the community centre using regular hexagon tiles (120° angles) and equilateral triangle tiles (60° angles). At one point on the border, exactly 2 hexagons meet. How many triangles are needed to fill the rest of the space around that point?
questions.explain: Angles around a point must total 360°: the hexagons use 2 × 120° = 240°, leaving 360° - 240° = 120°, and 120° ÷ 60° = 2 triangles. The common error is using 180° for a full turn instead of 360°, which gives too few triangles.

questions.question: Maya animates a salmon sticker on a grid. One point of the sticker starts at M(-3, 4). She first reflects the sticker in the x-axis, and then rotates the result 90° counterclockwise about the origin. Where does M end up?
questions.explain: Do the steps in order: the reflection in the x-axis sends (-3, 4) to (-3, -4), then the 90° counterclockwise rotation uses (x, y) to (-y, x), giving (4, -3). The big trap is that order matters — doing the rotation first would land the point at (-4, 3) instead.

questions.question: Nadia is laying regular octagon patio stones (each angle 135°) in her Kelowna backyard. She fits exactly 2 octagons together at each meeting point, but notices a gap. What shape exactly fills that gap, and why?
options: A square, because the gap measures 360° - 270° = 90°
An equilateral triangle, because the gap measures 180° - 135° = 45°
A regular pentagon, because the gap measures 108°
Nothing — three octagons meet exactly, so there is no gap
questions.explain: Angles around a point total 360°, so two octagons take 2 × 135° = 270° and the leftover gap is 90°, which is exactly a square corner. Two traps hide here: measuring the gap from 180° instead of 360°, and assuming octagons tessellate alone — 3 × 135° = 405°, which overlaps.
